hints: Focus on what makes a carbon chiral, a carbon joined to four completely different atoms or groups.
Look closely at carbon X, it has H, OH, the C=O part above and a chain below, so all four groups are different.
Now check Y the same way, then count the hydrogens on Z to see why it cannot be chiral.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for a chiral centre**

A chiral carbon must be sp3 and bonded to four different groups. If any two groups are the same, it is not chiral.

Rule to apply:
$$\text{chiral C = C with 4 different substituents}$$

**Check carbon X**

X is $\text{HO}-\text{C}-\text{H}$ joined to $\text{C=O}$ above and to $\text{CH(OH)}$ below. Its four groups are $-\text{H}$, $-\text{OH}$, $-\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $-\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$.

All four are different, so X is a chiral centre.

**Check carbon Y**

Y is $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{OH}$ joined to a different chain above and below. Its four groups are $-\text{H}$, $-\text{OH}$, the upper part containing X and the ketone, and the lower part containing $\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$.

All four are different, so Y is also a chiral centre.

**Check carbon Z and conclude**

Z is $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$ with $-\text{OH}$ below. It has two identical H atoms, so it has only three types of group.

Therefore Z is not chiral, and only X and Y from this list are chiral centres.

options.A: Incorrect. X and Y are chiral, but Z is $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with two H atoms attached. Two identical groups means it cannot be a chiral centre.
options.B: Correct. Both X and Y are attached to H, OH and two different carbon chain fragments, so each has four different groups. Z has two H atoms so is achiral.
options.C: Incorrect. X is indeed chiral, but Y is also chiral. Y has H, OH and two different up and down chain sections, so it should not be left out.
options.D: Incorrect. Y is chiral, but X is chiral too. X has H, OH, the $\text{C=O}$ group above and the rest of the sugar chain below, all different.
